summary: This informational RFC introduces transporting call control User-to-User Information in SIP and develops requirements for a new SIP mechanism. Some SIP sessions are tied to non-SIP applications that need to pass data between user agents.

eli5.summary: When a phone call is set up, sometimes a small note must ride along from one side to the other. This describes why and what is needed.

questions: how does sip uui differ from sip info
subtitle: Why some SIP calls need to carry an opaque note from one endpoint to the other, and what a solution must do.

tldr.problem: Some SIP sessions belong to a non-SIP application that needs a small piece of data passed between the two user agents at call setup, as ISDN User-to-User Information does in call centers today.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines call control UUI as opaque application data, walks through four call flows (user agent to user agent, proxy retargeting, redirection and referral) and derives 15 requirements for a new SIP mechanism.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement and requirements document only. It defines no protocol itself; it sets the bar that a later SIP extension has to meet.

facts.label: Minimum UUI size
facts.value: 128 octets of data plus 1 octet protocol discriminator (129 total)

today: RFC 6567 is Informational and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements only; the mechanism that meets them is defined elsewhere.

sections.title: What Call Control UUI Is
sections.content:
Some SIP sessions are set up by, or tied to, a non-SIP application. That application may have a small piece of information, the User-to-User Information (UUI), that must reach the other endpoint during session establishment. To SIP this data is opaque: it has nothing to do with SIP routing, authentication or any other SIP function, and SIP should not interpret it or operate on it. If a SIP element does need to understand the data, it is not UUI and needs another mechanism, such as a new header field.

The RFC gives two reasons for this definition. It keeps protocol layers strictly separate, and it is neither feasible nor desirable for a user agent to understand the data; it should just pass it to the application that does. As a result the mechanism creates no requirements on proxies, Back-to-Back User Agents or Session Border Controllers.
sections.eli5: The note is sealed in an envelope. The post office (SIP) carries it but never opens it. Only the person it is for reads it.

sections.title: ISDN Interworking and SIP INFO
sections.content:
The main driver is interworking with ISDN UUI, specifically the ITU-T Q.931 User-to-User Information Element and the Q.763 User-to-User Information Parameter. The RFC says ISDN UUI is widely used in the PSTN in contact centers and call centers, and those applications are moving from ISDN to SIP. Native SIP endpoints will need a similar service that can interwork with the ISDN one.

The RFC separates call control UUI from other UUI. SIP already has a way to send arbitrary data between user agents during a session or dialog: the SIP INFO method (RFC 6086). Call control UUI, in contrast, must be exchanged at setup time and carried in the INVITE and a few other methods and responses. Applications without that need can simply use SIP INFO and need no new extension.
sections.eli5: Call centers already attach little notes to phone calls on the old phone network. As they move to internet calls, they want to keep doing that. If the note can wait until the call is running, there is already a way. This is for notes needed right at the start.

sections.title: Four Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC walks through four call flows. In the first, user agent to user agent, the originating user agent puts UUI in the INVITE, which goes through a proxy to the terminating user agent. An ISDN gateway could map it into a DSS1, QSIG or ISUP element, or an application could show it to the user or use it for a screen pop. Normal proxy rules should forward it unmodified.

In proxy retargeting, a proxy changes the Request-URI of the INVITE, and the UUI has to pass through unchanged. In redirection, a Redirect Server inserts the UUI in a 3xx response and it is then included in the INVITE sent to the terminating user agent; the originating user agent need not support UUI but must support the redirection mechanism used. In referral, a referrer sends a REFER carrying UUI, which causes an INVITE with UUI to be generated.

The RFC calls redirection and referral the most important scenarios for contact centers, where incoming calls are almost always redirected or referred, sometimes several times. An Automatic Call Distributer acting as a Redirect Server is the example it gives.
sections.eli5: The note can travel straight to the other phone, survive being rerouted on the way, be stuck on by a receptionist who forwards you, or be attached by someone who tells you to call a third person.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
Section 3 lists REQ-1 to REQ-12 for the mechanism itself. The mechanism has to let user agents insert and receive UUI in INVITE requests and in 18x and 200 responses (REQ-1), in BYE and its 200 OK (REQ-2), and in redirects and referrals (REQ-3). UUI must survive proxy retargeting (REQ-4) and should not require anyone to dereference a URL (REQ-5). It must support interworking with DSS1, QSIG and ISUP (REQ-6).

A user agent client must be able to learn that a server understands the mechanism (REQ-7) and require it, so that the request fails if no such server is reachable (REQ-8). Proxies must be able to remove a particular application usage of UUI (REQ-9), and user agents must be able to discover which application usages another understands (REQ-10), which implies a registry of application usages. The ISDN protocol discriminator, the first octet of the data, plays that role there.

UUI is a sequence of octets, and the solution must carry at least 128 octets of user data plus a one-octet protocol discriminator, 129 octets in total (REQ-11). The recipient must be able to tell who inserted the UUI, though this may be implicit when there is only one other end (REQ-12).
sections.eli5: A good note system must work at the start and end of a call, survive rerouting, carry enough text, let phones check that the other side understands notes, and let border guards remove notes they do not like.

sections.title: Security Models and Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC says UUI security is provided jointly by the application layer and the SIP layer, and users should not assume a standardized but rarely deployed mechanism is in place. It describes three models. In the first, the SIP layer is untrusted and the application protects the UUI itself with integrity protection or encryption; the RFC notes that SIP end-to-end security has virtually no deployment. In the second, the application passes UUI unprotected and relies on SIP to secure it; this is possible in theory but of extremely limited practical use. In the third, a trust domain relies on perimeter security, hop-by-hop mechanisms and filtering at border elements, which is the model of the PSTN and ISDN where UUI is used today.

Three requirements follow. REQ-13: allow integrity protection of the UUI, noting a tradeoff with REQ-9 that hop-by-hop protection could resolve. REQ-14: allow end-to-end privacy of the UUI. REQ-15: allow both end-to-end and hop-by-hop security models, since the ISDN UUI service requires hop-by-hop.
sections.eli5: A sealed note can be locked by the sender, or the post offices can promise to guard it. The system should allow both.
